991.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
991.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state of one who has found the company of the holy: no one is an enemy or an outsider any more, and he is at ease with everyone. The Sikh institutions of the open langar and the sangat put this openness into practice.
991.tie_back: The Kural says courtesy comes easily to someone approachable by all, and Guru Arjan describes exactly that state of being on easy terms with everyone, with no one treated as a stranger.
991.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
991._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong thematic fit on openness to all, though the verse describes an inner spiritual state rather than the social virtue of approachability as such.

992.quote_or_event: “Recognize the Lord's Light within all, and do not consider social class or status; there are no classes or castes in the world hereafter.”
992.explanation: Guru Nanak tells his hearers to see God's light in everyone and not to ask about anyone's jaati (caste or birth status). Sikh teaching consistently refuses to treat lineage as a source of worth.
992.tie_back: The Kural names loving kindness and birth in a worthy family as the two roots of courtesy; Guru Nanak affirms the first, in recognising God's light in all, but rejects the second, refusing to weigh anyone by birth.
992.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 349, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
992._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a next-best match given candidly, because Sikh teaching explicitly rejects the Kural's appeal to noble family birth and shares only its emphasis on love toward all.

993.quote_or_event: “If you are indeed a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, then why didn't you come by some other way?”
993.explanation: Kabir mocks the claim of birth-superiority by pointing out that every human body comes into the world in the same way. Bodily sameness proves nobody is higher, and what distinguishes people has to lie elsewhere.
993.tie_back: The Kural says sameness of limbs does not make people truly alike and that real likeness is likeness of character, and Kabir likewise treats the shared body as settling nothing about a person's worth.
993.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 324, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
993._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a reasonable fit, since both look past the shared human body, though Kabir uses it to deny caste rank while the Kural uses it to stress likeness in character.

994.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
994.explanation: Guru Nanak places seva, selfless service done in the middle of ordinary life, at the centre of the Sikh path and promises it honour before God. Service of others is the Sikh form of being useful to the world.
994.tie_back: The Kural says the world praises those who are useful to others through justice and beneficence, and Guru Nanak likewise promises honour to those who serve in the midst of the world.
994.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
994._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a reasonable fit on service bringing honour, though the honour promised is in God's court rather than the world's praise, and justice is not named.

995.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all. Do not break anyone’s heart; these are all priceless jewels.”
995.explanation: Farid's saloks forbid even one harsh word because God lives in every person, and call every heart a priceless jewel that must not be broken. The next salok repeats that harming anyone's mind is never good.
995.tie_back: The Kural warns that mockery hurts even in jest and so the wise keep courtesy even toward enemies, and Farid likewise forbids any wounding word to anyone, since God dwells in all.
995.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 129 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
995._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strong fit on never wounding with words, though Farid speaks of harsh words in general rather than of ridicule in jest specifically.

996.quote_or_event: “That mortal who renounces possessiveness, greed, emotional attachment and egotism - says Nanak, he himself is saved, and he saves many others as well.”
996.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur teaches that the person who conquers ego and greed does not stop at their own freedom but becomes a means of others' deliverance too. In Sikh thought the Gurmukh's goodness steadies and uplifts those around them.
996.tie_back: The Kural says the world keeps going because it rests on people of good character, and Guru Tegh Bahadur likewise describes the selfless person as one who carries many others with them.
996.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, salok 22, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
996._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a partial fit, since the salok is about spiritual deliverance of others rather than the Kural's social claim that the world itself would sink without such people.

997.quote_or_event: “He acts like a beast, and does not understand anything. Practicing falsehood, he becomes false.”
997.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the manmukh, the self-willed person, as living at the level of an animal despite being human, because he lacks the understanding that makes human life worthwhile. Gurbani often uses the image of the beast for a human life emptied of its proper quality.
997.tie_back: The Kural says those without humane qualities are no better than trees however sharp their minds, and Guru Amar Das likewise says that a person without true understanding sinks to the level of a beast.
997.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1132, Raag Bhairao, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
997._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a next-best match, since the shared idea of a human sunk below the human is clear, but the Kural's contrast with a file-sharp intellect has no counterpart here.

998.quote_or_event: “Farid, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
998.explanation: Farid tells the devotee not to strike back even at someone who has struck him, but to answer with a gesture of humility and go home in peace. The Gurus kept this teaching in the scripture as a model of courtesy toward the hostile.
998.tie_back: The Kural calls it the lowest disgrace to fail in courtesy even toward the unfriendly and those who wrong us, and Farid asks for exactly that courtesy, even toward someone using his fists.
998.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, salok 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
998._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strong fit on keeping courtesy toward those who do us wrong, though Farid's emphasis is on non-retaliation and humility rather than the social grace the Kural calls courtesy.

999.quote_or_event: “If a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns appeared, even with such light, there would still be pitch darkness without the Guru.”
999.explanation: Guru Angad says that no amount of outer light can lift the darkness of a life without the Guru. Outward brightness and inner darkness can exist together.
999.tie_back: The Kural says the wide world lies in darkness even by day for those who cannot share in friendly cheer, and Guru Angad's verse uses the same paradox of darkness in the midst of light.
999.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 2, Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
999._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a next-best match on the image of darkness in daylight only, since Guru Angad's cause of darkness is the absence of the Guru, not the inability to share cheerful company.

1000.quote_or_event: “Wash the vessel, sit down and anoint it with fragrance; then, go out and get the milk. Add the rennet of clear consciousness to the milk of good deeds, and then, free of desire, let it curdle.”
1000.explanation: Guru Nanak takes the household work of setting milk to curd as an image of the spiritual life: the vessel, the inner self, must be cleaned first, or the milk of good deeds will not set into anything good.
1000.tie_back: The Kural says great wealth in the hands of a discourteous person is like good milk spoiled by an unclean vessel, and Guru Nanak uses the very same image of a clean vessel needed before good milk can turn out well.
1000.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 728, Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1000._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong match on the milk-and-vessel image, though Guru Nanak's milk is good deeds and the vessel the mind, where the Kural's milk is wealth and the vessel a person's character.
